region: United Kingdom (England, Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland) with the Channel Islands and the Isle of Man
method: Spot list from the Surfnerd country and county/council pages (surf-reports/united-kingdom/*, surf-reports/ireland/*, surf-reports/jersey, /guernsey, /isle-of-man) and the Surf-Forecast.com country break lists (countries/United-Kingdom/breaks, countries/Ireland/breaks), plus a Wannasurf crawl (spot/Europe/UK, spot/Europe/Ireland). Facts from each Surfnerd .md page and the matched Surf-Forecast.com and Wannasurf pages (matched by name within 4 km), fetched about 1 request a second per site. Facing only from Surfnerd "Faces X"; a spot without it is dropped. Nearest sources: wave buoys from the Channel Coastal Observatory public real-time pages (position and latest time read from each station page; the CCO API needs a key and was not used), the Marine Institute ERDDAP (IWBNetwork, IWaveBNetwork), NDBC activestations.xml international partners (UK Met Office, Met Eireann, States of Jersey; live = wave height in latest_obs.txt) and EMODnet Physics platform metadata (Cefas WaveNet, Met Office and others not already listed, deduplicated within 2 km); tide gauges from the Environment Agency flood-monitoring API (England; live = latest reading on or after 2026-11-08), the Marine Institute Irish National Tide Gauge Network, CCO tide stations, and the IOC Sea Level Station Monitoring Facility (UK and Ireland); tide predictions from the Marine Institute imiTidePrediction (Ireland and Northern Ireland spots); airports from the Iowa Environmental Mesonet GB__ASOS and IE__ASOS networks (online flag). Cefas WaveNet has no public station JSON (login for data); its buoys appear here through EMODnet. UKHO tide predictions need a subscription and are not listed. Distances are great-circle from the spot pin.

facts.overview: Sunderland sits on the Northeast England coast, north of the mouth of the Wear. It isn't one of the region's classic breaks, but it's a fun spot when it's on. A long, curved breakwater at Roker Beach shapes the waves: a right wedges off the northern side of the wall in small, clean swells, while inside the rivermouth on the other side of the breakwater a peak fires short rights and longer lefts, but only in massive swells. facts.overview: Croyde Beach is a high-quality, hollow, peaky beachbreak on the North Devon coast, hemmed in by Downend Point to the south and Baggy Point to the north. The average surf runs a little smaller than Cornwall, but at six foot Croyde delivers Hossegor-like power. (surfnerd)

facts.overview: Bude Summerleaze is a broad beachbreak on a long stretch of golden sand, edged by a breakwater and river at the southern end of the bay. It holds some decent sandbars, including a quality low-tide left and a high-tide right near the seawater swimming pool at the northern edge. The bottom is a mix of sand and rock, and at higher tides you can find a little shelter from strong wind and swell near the mouth of the harbour. (surfnerd)

facts.overview: Shoreham is a beach break set around a harbour arm and power station, where the sandbar is anchored by the power-station outfall. Its best-known peak, the Hotpipe, is the outflow from the nearby power plant, sitting on the eastern outside of the harbour arm at the most consistent end of a series of lefts and rights. In big storm conditions the wave also breaks inside the harbour arm itself, sheltered from the wind and funnelled between concrete walls to throw up both rights and lefts, an almost proto-wavepool setup. It rates below average overall, but delivers fun waves when the Channel comes to life. (surfnerd)

facts.overview: Brighton - Marina is a fickle chalk and flint reef break tucked into the eastern corner of the marina, where the pier shelters a sheltered pocket from southwest gales. That shelter is really the whole story here: this is a storm-swell spot that only comes to life when it's blowing hard. When it does, the reef throws both lefts and rights that can run long and fun, though they tend to be slow and fat, reforming as they roll rather than lining up cleanly. It's a below-average break most of the time, but it earns its regulars on the right day. (surfnerd)

facts.overview: Constantine is a consistent beachbreak set in a crescent-shaped bay that opens into a half-mile stretch of golden sand at low tide. Sandbars in the middle of the bay throw up the main peaks, while a left-hand reef breaks over rocks near the headland at the southern end. facts.overview: Holywell Bay is a pretty, crescent-shaped, dune-backed beachbreak that makes a quieter alternative to Newquay. It's rarely surfed and fairly fickle: on its day it serves up fun sandbar lefts and rights, but it can just as easily close out down the beach. The southern fringe of the bay, marked by the twin Gull Rocks, cuts off a lot of swell, so it really comes alive when a larger swell is lighting up nearby breaks. When the river shapes the banks well, the sand can hold genuinely good waves. (surfnerd)

facts.overview: Penhale, also known as Perran Sands, is a huge stretch of golden sand backed by towering dunes, with a consistent and fun beach break that throws up shifting peaks. facts.tide: Works at High (Best at High, Better on rising). High tide is the call, and a rising tide is generally the better window as the sandbar starts to reform the wave. (surfnerd); High tide only, Rising and falling tides (wannasurf)
facts.bottom: Uneven Reef, Sand (surfnerd); Sandy with rock (wannasurf)

facts.overview: Vazon Bay - Centres sits in the middle of Vazon Bay, one of several distinct breaks along this stretch and the hub of the Guernsey surf scene. Solid swells break on a rarely surfed outer reef peak in the centre of the bay, then reform into a fast, hollow right on the sandbar inside. The bottom is a mix of uneven reef and sand, and it throws both lefts and rights. Rocks are part of the setup here, so keep them in mind when you pick your line. (surfnerd)

facts.overview: Brimms Ness - The Cove is the middle of three reefs on the Brims Ness headland in Caithness, tucked between the fast, barreling right of the Bowl and the long walling lefts of the Point. facts.overview: Porth Neigwl, better known as Hells Mouth, is North Wales' best-known spot. Sitting at the end of the Llyn Peninsula, it's a perfectly positioned swell catcher, and its sandy beach turns raw swell into good quality waves. It fires up when a low pressure parks to the south off Biscay and the swell funnels between the Irish and Welsh coastlines to light up this long bay. At the southern end you'll find The Corner, a wedgy left-hander that peaks and peels along a rocky bottom before finishing on sand. To the north sits The Reef, a busy right-hander, with plenty of beach break peaks scattered in between. On its day it's excellent, serving up crowded but genuinely good, wedgy peaks. (surfnerd)

facts.overview: Llantwit Major is a large, triangular reef where the wave changes character as the tide moves. It's a right-hander that breaks over a mix of uneven reef and sand, so the shape shifts depending on how much water is covering the ledge. (surfnerd)
